english: One more penalty. If Gonzalo Montiel scores, Argentina will become world champion.

By the centre line the captain stands, arms around his teammates. He is thirty-five. He has lost four finals with the national team, and six years ago he said he was leaving it. This World Cup final in Qatar is most likely his last chance.
Montiel runs up, and the captain looks at the sky. Where he points after almost every goal, for his grandmother.
Twenty-five years before that night, a doctor in Rosario realised the boy was hardly growing. And every evening he himself injected his leg with a thin needle.
Almost four years after Qatar, Argentina again played in a World Cup final. Two days later he sat down and wrote a short message. In it were two words in Spanish. Me vacié. I gave everything.
He was never talkative. He just played. How did a quiet boy, too small, carry a whole country? It all began on a small pitch in Rosario, when a team was one player short.
In that message he also thanked his family. Without them there would have been no career. And the first to believe in him was his grandmother.
It was a small neighbourhood club, Grandoli, in Rosario, in Argentina. Coach Salvador Aparicio was looking for anyone at all who could play.
At the edge of the pitch stood a woman named Celia. She had come to the game of her grandson Matías. And she had brought his little brother, a little one of about four or five.
She pointed at the little one. The coach looked at him and had doubts. The boy was tiny, much smaller than the others. But Celia did not give up and kept asking the coach to put him on.
In the end Aparicio agreed. He put the boy on the wing, next to Celia, and said: if he cries, take him away.

At first he barely touched the ball. But when the ball came to him again, he took it with his left and dribbled past one boy after another. He did not cry. Later he recalled that he scored two goals that day.
In the first game the other boys were two or three years older. Some were almost twice as big. But it did not matter.
Aparicio never took him off again. And from that day it was Celia who took him to every training and every game.

That boy was Lionel Andrés Messi. He was born in Rosario on the twenty-fourth of June 1987, the third son of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother was also called Celia, like his grandmother. His father worked at a steel plant. His mother worked in a small workshop that made magnets.
He had two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Later a little sister, María Sol, joined the family.
Rosario is a working city on the Paraná river: factories, a port and two clubs that split it in half. Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.

The family lived in a simple house in the south of the city, in the La Bajada district. He and his brothers played in the street until dark. Lionel was always the smallest of them and always the one with the ball.
He went to an ordinary school near home, school number sixty-six. Years later a mural with his face appeared in the neighbourhood. It says he is from another galaxy and from this neighbourhood.
At home everyone called him Leo. Later, because he was so small and quick, relatives and teammates gave him another name. La Pulga. The Flea.
His mother said that at home he could be cheeky and stubborn. He hated losing, even at cards. But on the pitch that stubbornness kept him from giving up the fight for the ball.
His father and brothers supported Newell's Old Boys, the red-and-black half of the city. On match days the whole family went to the stadium together. Leo already knew where he wanted to play.
At six he joined the family's favourite club, Newell's Old Boys. In one of the first games they won six-nil. Four were his.
The boys born in 1987 became a team people in Rosario still talk about. It was called "La Máquina del '87", the Machine of eighty-seven. For years it almost never lost.
Sometimes opponents asked in advance: if the score reached six-nil, the game would just be stopped. But even at six-nil Lionel got angry if he had not scored himself.

Coach Carlos Marconi often tells this story. He promised Leo an alfajor, a sweet chocolate biscuit, for every goal. Leo scored so many that Marconi changed the deal: two alfajores, but only for a header. Soon the smallest one scored a header. He turned to Marconi and, smiling, held up two fingers.
Teammates remember the little things. Before every game he carefully cleaned his boots and taped his own ankles, like a professional. And he was eight or nine.
One of them recalls a derby with Rosario Central. Leo beat one defender again and again, until that boy's father shouted to his son from the stands: hit him!
The league kept count of his goals. More than two hundred in five years. And in Rosario they say there were really many more.
His height always got in the way. Big defenders kicked his legs, and some parents shouted: stop him at any cost! Every time he got up and asked for the ball again.
Coaches protected him. They asked him to pass earlier so he would not get hurt. But he kept dribbling. If he lost the ball, he immediately ran to win it back.
But in 1998, when he was ten, grandmother Celia died. The one who brought him to football was gone.
Later he said he loved her very much and that it is still hard for him to talk about her. He dedicates goals to her. After many of them he points to the sky.
His mother said that after Celia's death he talked to his grandmother and asked for help. Few people knew about it. He rarely talked about feelings.
Without her he kept playing. He was still the best in the team. But something was wrong, and everyone saw it. The other boys were growing, and he was not.
Newell's sent him to endocrinologist Diego Schwarzstein. The club wanted to understand why its best young player was much smaller than the others.
Tests showed his body produced little growth hormone. Without treatment he would have grown ten to fifteen centimetres shorter.
One word would haunt him for years. Small. The best of his age in Rosario, and the smallest.
There was a treatment: a small injection in the legs, every evening, without breaks. It was very expensive, more than nine hundred dollars a month.
While still a child he learned to give the injections himself. Every evening the same thing: needle in the leg. A teammate remembers him doing it before games, as if it were nothing.
Once a friend's father taught him to drive on a quiet country road. Leo was eleven.

And every month his father counted the money. The medicine ate a huge part of his factory wage. Help from insurance and the club soon ran out. And without treatment his son's football would have ended before it really began.
A club that would pay was needed. Lionel went to Buenos Aires for a trial at River Plate, one of the biggest clubs in the country.
In 2026 Messi told the story himself. He trained there about ten days, and River wanted to keep him and even pay for the treatment. But first Newell's had to release him.
He was never closer to playing for a big club in his home country.
But Newell's did not release him, and River's offer was lost. That was the end of it, he said. And then help came from the other side of the ocean.

An Argentine agent in Barcelona was sent videos of a boy from Rosario. With another agent he showed them to the club, and Barcelona invited the boy for a trial. In September 2000 Lionel and his father flew to Spain. He was thirteen.
At Newell's they did not know where he had disappeared to. They said he was ill.
In Barcelona he played with older boys. Sporting director Carles Rexach came to watch.
They say that walking from the stand to the pitch should have taken Rexach three or four minutes. It took him fifteen: he could not take his eyes off the boy.
At the trial was also Cesc Fàbregas, who later played with Messi for years. Before the game the coach told him to mark the newcomer from Argentina. And to mark him hard.
Cesc took a look and decided: this will be easy. The boy is tiny. An instant later Fàbregas is on the ground, and the little Argentine runs away with the ball.

Rexach later said he told the club: sign him, don't even think about it. But the bosses had doubts. The boy was a foreigner, very small, and needed expensive treatment. Weeks passed and still there was no decision.
For Jorge the waiting was agonising. He had left a secure job at the factory. He lived with his son in a hotel in a foreign city and did not know whether they would have a home here.
After waiting more than two months, Jorge phoned Rexach and said directly: if it is not settled soon, they are going home.
On the fourteenth of December 2000 Rexach met the agents at a tennis club. No paper could be found, and he wrote a promise on a napkin. Barcelona will sign Lionel Messi.
One of the club's directors, Joan Gaspart, admitted: the napkin had no legal force. It was a way to calm a father ready to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed it, and both agents as witnesses. Years later the napkin was sold at auction in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
Barcelona promised to pay for the treatment and give the father a job. In February 2001 the whole family moved to Spain.
At thirteen Leo did not really understand what it all meant. He knew one thing: he would play, and the injections would continue, now paid for by Barcelona.
For the boy from La Bajada it was a dream. And for his family, the start of the hardest year of their lives.
Things did not go as dreamed. Because of rules for foreigners Lionel could not play officially for months. And in only his second game for the juniors he broke his leg.
His mother, brothers and little sister were homesick. They never settled in the new city and already in the first year decided to go back to Rosario.
Jorge asked his son whether he wanted to go back with them. Lionel said no. Later he put it into one sentence: I wanted to keep going, and Dad stayed with me.
And the family was split between two continents. Lionel and his father stayed in Barcelona. Part of Jorge's salary went on living there. The rest went to Rosario, to his wife and other children.
Now a thirteen-year-old boy lived eleven thousand kilometres from his mother, brothers and sister.
On Sundays there was nobody around. He played video games with his father in a small flat. And then, writes biographer Guillem Balagué, he went to his room and cried into his pillow.
My old man was always there, Messi said later, and we went through a lot of bad things together.
At the club he hardly spoke. At the first training the coach asked where he played. He mumbled one word, "forward", and sat in a corner of the dressing room.
His teammates did not know what to think. According to Fàbregas, for a long time they thought he could not speak. He could. He was just very shy. He spoke little. He just played.
They called him "el enano", shorty. But when the ball came to him, nobody laughed.

Little by little he found his place. In his team there were many boys born in 1987 like him: Cesc Fàbregas, Gerard Piqué and others. They played with three defenders and attacked all the time. People started calling them the "Kids' Dream Team".
Gradually the quiet boy started joking with the others. It turned out he was funny and loved cards and video games. He hated losing at them as much as at football.
In a season they hardly lost, and Messi scored more than thirty goals. Tall Piqué looked out for him on the pitch.

Their coach, Tito Vilanova, later became one of the most important people in Messi's life. They say that once his team led three-nil after three minutes. Tito joked to his assistant: what will we tell them at half-time when it's eight-nil?
Every evening, injections. And every year he grew a little. By his teens the treatment had done its job.
In the end his height would be about one metre seventy. One of the shortest on the pitch. But it would be enough.
Many years later his doctor from Rosario, Diego Schwarzstein, said simply: I only helped a boy grow. Messi did everything else himself.
In November 2003 Barcelona played a friendly in Porto, at a stadium opening. Coach Frank Rijkaard put on sixteen-year-old Lionel Messi. On the other bench sat José Mourinho.
It was only a friendly. But the boy had already played for the first team. In one season he went through four of the club's teams, one after another.
Official debut: the sixteenth of October 2004, against Espanyol. He came on near the end wearing number thirty. He was seventeen.
He then became Barcelona's youngest player in the Spanish league. Later others broke the record. And he spent seventeen years at Barcelona.
At the club they remember that off the pitch he was shy and almost silent. And one agent said he had never seen a footballer with thinner legs.
But one person in the dressing room already saw what he could do. The best player in the world, Ronaldinho, took the quiet one under his wing.

Other Brazilians, Deco, Sylvinho and Thiago Motta, also looked after the newcomer. Ronaldinho sat next to him in the dressing room and invited him to the Brazilians' table. Leo said he learned a lot from them, but most of all from him.
Not everyone was kind. Frenchman Ludovic Giuly recalled that some of the older players kicked the boy in training, to see what he would do. He did not complain. He got up and kept playing.
On the first of May 2005, against Albacete, Messi came on for the last minutes. Ronaldinho lifted the ball over the defence, and Messi lobbed it over the goalkeeper. The referee called offside.
A few moments later Ronaldinho did exactly the same. And Messi did exactly the same. This time the goal counted.
Ronaldinho bent down, and the boy jumped on his back. First official goal for Barcelona. Ronaldinho is proud he was there at the start of this story.

Let's pause for a moment. A few words about me. I'm Kamil. I'm twenty-one, and I've been starting YouTube channels since 2014, since I was nine. Almost none of them took off. A hundred thousand subscribers and the silver button is my childhood dream. If this story means something to you, subscribing will bring me closer to it. And now, on we go.
In spring 2006 Barcelona reached the Champions League knockouts, and Messi tormented Chelsea at Stamford Bridge. Two weeks later, in the return match, he tore a thigh muscle and left in tears.
The whole Camp Nou stood and applauded him. Rijkaard hugged him. Messi was eighteen.
Barcelona won the final in Paris. Messi did not play. He was so upset that he did not celebrate with everyone. Later he said he deeply regrets that night.
Back in 2004 another question came up. Messi had lived in Spain since thirteen, and the Spanish football federation was calling him to its national team.
Argentina's youth team coaches found out and hurried. In June 2004 they organised a friendly with Paraguay, largely so that Messi would play for his homeland.
Argentina won eight-nil. Messi said the Spain option was real. But at heart he was from Rosario.
Old academy friend Cesc Fàbregas said it would have been amazing if Leo had played for Spain. Soon Spain won the World Cup without him. And Argentina waited for a trophy another eleven years.
In 2005 at the youth World Cup in the Netherlands he became the best player of the tournament. He scored six goals, including two penalties in the final against Nigeria. Argentina: world champions.
He received the Golden Ball and Golden Boot as the tournament's best player and top scorer. For the first time the boy from Rosario became a champion in the white-and-sky-blue shirt.
Six weeks later, in August 2005, he debuted for the senior national team in a friendly with Hungary in Budapest. He came on in the second half.

As soon as he touched the ball, a defender grabbed his shirt. Messi pulled his arm free, and his arm hit the defender. The referee showed a red card. He was on the pitch less than a minute. They say he left in tears.
Later he told what he was thinking: I came on, I was sent off, and they will never call me up again.
One of his teammates that evening ran to argue with the referee for him. His name was Lionel Scaloni. Remember that name: years later he will return to this story.
He was called up again. In March 2006, against Croatia, he scored his first goal for Argentina. And in the summer he went to his first World Cup, in Germany.
Against Serbia and Montenegro he came on as a sub and scored the sixth goal of six. At eighteen he became the youngest Argentine to score at a World Cup.
In that game he also gave an assist to Hernán Crespo. He already played like one of them.
In the quarter-final against the hosts, Germany, Argentina were leading. But the coach made his last substitutions without bringing him on, and the game slipped away. Argentina went out on penalties.
Messi sat on the bench the whole match. For the first time a World Cup ended and he could only watch. He said nothing to the press. Again almost wordless.
In April 2007, in the Copa del Rey semi-final against Getafe, Messi got the ball in his own half. He beat one, a second, a third, then the goalkeeper, and scored.
He started on the right, near the centre line. In about ten seconds he ran almost the whole pitch, and the ball seemed glued to his left foot.
All of Argentina recognised this goal. Diego Maradona, the country's greatest hero, scored almost the same goal against England at the 1986 World Cup. Messi was nineteen.
Barcelona won that match five-two. But in the return game Getafe won four-nil. Even such a goal did not save Barça from elimination.
For Barcelona these were difficult years. Ronaldinho was fading, the team was losing, the club was looking for a fresh start. Messi played better and better but was often injured.
In the message after the 2026 final there is one more line: I swear I always gave everything. And so it was. But for many years with the national team even that was not enough to win.
In summer 2007 at the Copa América in Venezuela, Argentina reached the final against Brazil. Messi had just turned twenty. Brazil won three-nil.
He played all ninety minutes and could do almost nothing. At the end he watched Brazil celebrate.
It was his first final with the senior team. Nobody knew he would lose three more before he won one.
In 2008 he wanted to play at the Olympics in Beijing. Barcelona did not want to release him: the Games were not in the official football calendar. The matter went to the sports court.
Messi said it was his decision, because he would never have another Olympics. The court sided with the clubs.
But Barcelona had a new coach, Pep Guardiola. He himself had won Olympic gold in Barcelona in 1992. He understood and let him go.
At those Games he scored twice, against Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.

In the final against Nigeria, in front of almost ninety thousand spectators, his pass sent his friend Ángel Di María through on goal, and he lobbed the goalkeeper. The only goal of the match. Argentina took Olympic gold.

Later he said some things in football happen once in a lifetime. And this was his only Olympics. He calls that gold one of his most precious wins. And in Barcelona Guardiola was preparing a new role for him.
Guardiola's first decision surprised everyone. He told Ronaldinho, Messi's idol, that he no longer counted on him. Barcelona would be built around the twenty-one-year-old.
That summer Ronaldinho left for Milan. Before leaving he told Leo to take his number ten. The quiet boy who had once jumped on his back now wore his number and became the team's star.
In May 2009 Barcelona came to the Bernabéu to play Real. According to journalist Martí Perarnau's book, the day before Guardiola called Messi in and showed him a video.
Between Real's midfield and defence there was empty space. Guardiola told him to start on the right and then drift into the centre, into that space. And with the ball, run straight at goal.
According to the same book, Guardiola kept the plan secret until the last moment.
Messi played neither on the wing nor in the centre, but somewhere in between. The defenders did not understand who should follow him. Barcelona won six-two in Madrid. Messi scored twice.
Soon after, in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barça were losing in the ninety-third minute. Messi passed to Andrés Iniesta, who scored. Barcelona in the final.
Three weeks later in Rome they played Manchester United in the Champions League final. Before the game Guardiola showed them a video of the season set to music from "Gladiator".
Before the final Leo remembered Paris: back then he felt left out and did not celebrate. This time, he said, he needed to celebrate much more.
In the seventieth minute Xavi crossed into the box. The smallest man on the pitch jumped highest and headed it over goalkeeper Edwin van der Sar.
Van der Sar was almost two metres tall. Messi, about one metre seventy. And the "too small" one won in the air.
Barça won two-nil.
That year they won everything possible. The league, the cup, the Champions League and three more trophies. Six out of six: no team had done that.
The sixth came in December, in Abu Dhabi, against Argentina's Estudiantes. In extra time Messi scored the winner with his chest.
Shortly before that he received his first Ballon d'Or, the prize for the best player in the world. He was twenty-two. The boy who had been too small became the best.
In January 2011 at the Ballon d'Or ceremony in Zurich, all three finalists came from one school, Barcelona's academy, La Masia. Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
Many expected Xavi or Iniesta to win. They had just become world champions with Spain, and Iniesta scored the final's winning goal. But Messi won, for the second year running.
He said he did not expect it. And that Xavi and Iniesta deserved the prize no less, perhaps more. They were the first to congratulate him.
The three of them gave a press conference, and all said the same thing. This prize is for the team.
Later Xavi recalled meeting him on a trip: a polite, modest guy, not at all a show-off. He never thought he would become the best player in history.

In May 2011 at Wembley Barcelona again beat Manchester United in the Champions League final, and Messi scored with a powerful low shot from outside the box. But the most touching part was at the end. That spring defender Éric Abidal had had a liver tumour removed. Carles Puyol gave him the captain's armband so that he would be the one to lift the cup.

In May 2012 Guardiola led Barcelona at home for the last time. Messi scored all four goals. After the fourth he ran to the touchline to hug him. Guardiola joked that Leo had outshone everyone all season and it was impossible even to be jealous of him.
And in December 2012 he broke a forty-year-old record. Gerd Müller scored eighty-five goals in a calendar year. Messi finished the year with ninety-one, five of them in one Champions League match.

Müller was not offended. He called Leo a giant and joked that he had one flaw: he did not play for Bayern. Soon Leo sent him a Barcelona shirt with a handwritten note: with respect and admiration, a hug. Leo himself said titles matter more to him than records.
Life off the pitch changed too. His girlfriend was Antonela Roccuzzo from Rosario, whom he had known since childhood. In November 2012 their first son was born. They named him Thiago.
Two months after Thiago was born, Leo said fatherhood changes a person completely. His son is now the most important thing.

In January 2013 he won his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row. Nobody had won it four times. But that winter Tito Vilanova was again being treated for cancer. The same coach from La Masia, now he led the first team. And Abidal had just returned after a liver transplant. In his speech in Zurich Leo forgot to thank them. Afterwards he apologised. Tito, he said, believed in him when Leo was a kid who often sat on the bench.
In Barcelona he was a god. But with the national team everything was very different.
Argentina had not won a major trophy since 1993, when Messi was six. Now the whole country expected him to change that.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, Argentina was coached by Diego Maradona himself. In the quarter-final in Cape Town they played Germany. The Germans scored in the third minute and won four-nil. Messi did not score once in the tournament.
After the game Maradona said he had seen Messi in tears in the dressing room.
And whoever says this shirt doesn't matter to him is a fool.
Because that is exactly what many in Argentina said. At thirteen he left for Spain. He did not play for an Argentine club. He did not even sing the anthem before matches.
For such people there was a special expression: "pecho frío". Cold chest. Someone who feels little when it matters. To many, his silence seemed like indifference.
At the 2011 Copa América, at home, his own fans booed him. His father said his son was very hurt; he did not understand why.

The national coach at that Copa, Sergio Batista, tried to use him like Barcelona did. It did not work. Messi said comparing Argentina with Barça was a mistake. There they had played together for years.
Argentina went out in the quarter-final, on penalties, to Uruguay. At home the criticism did not die down. And he did what he always did. He spoke little. He just played.
In April 2014 Tito Vilanova died. He was forty-five. According to his assistant, six days before that Leo visited him and they talked for hours. The coach of his first great team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the World Cup in Brazil, Messi carried the team. After the first goal, against Bosnia, he looked at the sky, as he often did. In the group he scored four goals. Against Iran, the winner, in the ninety-first minute.
Four times he was man of the match. For the first time in twenty-four years Argentina was in a World Cup final.
In the semi-final they got past the Netherlands on penalties. Defender Javier Mascherano said that without Leo Argentina would not have got so far.
The final was at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro, again against Germany. Messi and his teammates had chances. Nobody scored. And in extra time Mario Götze scored.
After the whistle Messi was given the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player. On the way to get it he walked past the World Cup trophy and did not even glance at it.
He said this prize did not matter to him. Then FIFA president Sepp Blatter later claimed Messi kept repeating to himself: best, but not champion.
A second lost final. Three years later he said: this defeat stays with me forever.

In 2015 at the Copa América in Chile, Argentina reached the final again. Against Chile, even after a hundred and twenty minutes it was nil-nil. Messi scored his penalty. Two teammates missed, and Chile won.
Just a month before that he had again won the Champions League with Barcelona, in Berlin, together with Neymar and Luis Suárez. With the club he won everything. With the national team he lost.
Chile's team in that final was coached by an Argentine, Jorge Sampaoli. Two years later he would take over Argentina.
After that final Messi wrote that there is nothing more painful in football than a lost final. There were already three.
In June 2016 there was another chance. A special Copa América in the USA, a hundred years after the first. The final was at MetLife Stadium near New York.
And the opponent again was Chile. And again nobody scored. And again it went to penalties.
Messi took the first. He leaned back, and the ball flew high over the bar.
Chile won the shoot-out. It was his fourth lost final with the national team. Three in a row, in three years.
Lucas Biglia's penalty was also saved. But everyone remembered the captain's miss.
A few minutes later, in the tunnel, a journalist stopped him. The quiet man said only a couple of words: that's it, I'm finished with the national team.
His teammates were crushed. Sergio Agüero was his best friend in the team; for years they shared a room. Agüero said the defeat simply broke Leo.
Messi cried on his shoulder for about twenty-five seconds, like a little boy, and kept repeating: this isn't for me, this isn't for me.
And at night, according to the fitness coach, he found Leo at two o'clock: he was not sleeping and was sobbing.

And then something happened he did not expect. In Argentina people began asking him to stay. The country's president called and said publicly that Messi is the best thing Argentina has. And on a rainy Saturday in Buenos Aires hundreds of people came to the Obelisk with signs. "Don't go, Leo".
Somewhere in Argentina fifteen-year-old Enzo Fernández also wrote him a letter: don't go. Six years later Enzo would play next to him in a World Cup final.
The country that had called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later he announced: I'm coming back. And scored straight away.
He was asked why he came back. He said: I love the country and this shirt too much, I want to help.
Later he explained why he had wanted to leave. It was not only the pain of defeats, he said. Many things outside football had also hurt him and his family.
He admitted he does not even remember whether he told his father before announcing it in the tunnel. In that moment there was simply no other way.
That same summer a court in Spain found Messi and his father guilty of not paying taxes on income from image rights. Prison was replaced with fines, as often happens in Spain.
Messi told the court his father handled the money. By then the family had already paid back about five million euros.

In June 2017 Leo married Antonela in Rosario, the city of their childhood. He could have held the wedding anywhere, but he chose home. About two hundred and fifty guests came, among them teammates from Barcelona and the national team. Thiago and his younger brother Mateo sat in the front row, and Leo's brothers and sister were witnesses.

And the national team had problems. Before the last World Cup 2018 qualifier it was even outside the qualifying places. They needed a win in Quito, high in the Andes, where they had not won for sixteen years.

That evening Argentina's streets were nearly empty. People watched the match in bars and at home. In La Plata, U2 even delayed a concert so fans could watch the game on big screens. And in the first minute Ecuador scored, and the bars fell silent.
And then Messi scored three. Argentina won three-one and went to Russia. Even Ecuador fans applauded him.
In the dressing room they sang a song to spite the critics. Mascherano said that without the World Cup, for many it would all have been over.
Messi said not going to the World Cup would have been madness. Now his soul is at peace.
Coach Jorge Sampaoli said something many remembered: Messi does not owe Argentina a World Cup. Football owes Messi a World Cup.
Russia did not repay the debt. In the first game, against Iceland, Messi missed a penalty.
The goalkeeper who saved it, Hannes Halldórsson, was also a film director. He said he had studied Messi's penalties in advance.
Then they lost to Croatia nil-three. They beat Nigeria; Messi scored. A huge relief, he said.
In the round of sixteen, against France in Kazan, Antonela, Thiago and Mateo were in the stands in shirts saying "Papá". Argentina lost three-four. Messi again left with nothing.

In the 2026 farewell message he wrote that leaving the national team hurt and still hurts his soul. He already knew such pain, in Barcelona. There the end began with a few European nights the club does not want to remember.
Everything started to break. In 2018 they easily beat Roma at home, and in Rome lost nil-three. A year later it all repeated: three-nil against Liverpool at home and nil-four in Liverpool.
A couple of days after Anfield he said the coach was not to blame. The players were to blame above all.
In 2019 he took his sixth Ballon d'Or, the most of anyone. But that did not save what was collapsing around him.
And in August 2020 in Lisbon, Bayern crushed Barcelona eight-two.
Ten days after Lisbon Messi officially wrote to the club that he wanted to leave. Barcelona refused: the contract did not allow it.
His father flew to Barcelona for talks. In the end Messi stayed one more year: he would never go to court against his beloved club.
Six weeks after Lisbon Barcelona pushed out Luis Suárez, one of his best friends. Leo wrote that Suárez deserved a proper farewell, not being thrown out. But nothing surprises him any more.
And in November 2020 Diego Maradona died. Argentina mourned for many days. The man who had defended Messi after Cape Town was gone, and the country still had not won a major trophy with Messi.
That year the world closed down in lockdown because of the pandemic. And in summer 2021 the Copa América was moved to Brazil at the last moment. The final was at the Maracanã, against Brazil.
Because of the pandemic there were almost no spectators in the stadium. One of the most important matches of his national-team life took place in near silence.
The players had not seen their families for weeks. Before the final, in the dressing room, the captain who rarely spoke stood up. Someone filmed it.
For years they said he was too quiet to be a leader. That night he found his voice.

Forty-five days without family, guys, he said. He mentioned goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez, who had become a father and had not yet held his newborn daughter. And he finished: let's go out confident and calm, we're taking this cup home.
Martínez later said he wanted to cry. Another player admitted he was soon crying and does not remember the rest.
In the twenty-second minute Rodrigo De Paul found Ángel Di María with a long pass, the same friend from the Olympics. Di María lobbed the goalkeeper. One-nil.
For the next seventy minutes Brazil attacked and Argentina held on. Messi could have scored a second but missed. Never mind.
At the final whistle Messi fell to his knees, covering his face with his hands. Teammates ran over and jumped on top until he disappeared under them.
Then he called his wife and sons in Rosario. After four lost finals he had finally won a trophy with the senior national team. He was thirty-four.

After the game Di María said the curse had to fall one day, and now it had. Messi dedicated the title to his family, to the people of Argentina and to Maradona, who, he said, was surely cheering for them wherever he was.
A month later he was going to extend his contract with Barcelona. But the club announced that because of debts and Spanish league rules it could not keep him.
On the eighth of August 2021 he walked into a hall at Camp Nou to say goodbye. Before he could say a word, he started crying.
He said he was not ready for this. He and his family wanted to stay. He came here at thirteen and was leaving at thirty-four, with three sons, Thiago, Mateo and Ciro, born here.
It was also sad that he would not say goodbye to the fans. Because of the pandemic he had not seen them for a year and a half.
He moved to Paris Saint-Germain. It did not work out. After defeats the fans booed him.
Once, after a defeat, he flew to Saudi Arabia for promotional work without the club's permission. He was suspended; he apologised in a video. Everyone already understood he would not stay.

In November 2022 Argentina arrived at the World Cup in Qatar unbeaten in thirty-six matches. The coach was Lionel Scaloni, the same teammate from Budapest. Messi was thirty-five. Everyone understood: this was probably the last chance.
In the first game, against Saudi Arabia, he scored a penalty. Then the Saudis scored twice in five minutes. Argentina lost one-two. One of the biggest upsets in World Cup history.

After the game Messi came out to the journalists. There are no excuses, he said. In the dressing room there was dead silence. But he asked Argentina to believe in the team: we will be united as never before.
The players recalled: he talked to them more than ever. The quiet captain spoke up loudly.
And a song followed them everywhere. Fans called it "Muchachos". It was sung on the bus and in the dressing room, and Messi sang along.
From then on every game was a final. Against Mexico Messi opened the scoring, Argentina won two-nil. Then came Poland and Australia.
Against Australia he played the thousandth match of his career. And scored.
In the quarter-final against the Netherlands Argentina led two-nil, but the Dutch equalised in the last seconds. It went to penalties, and Argentina won.
After that game the world saw a Messi it had never seen. During a TV interview a Dutch player walked past, and Messi threw at him in Rosario street language: "What are you looking at, silly?"

The "cold" one was now unrecognisable. In the semi-final Argentina beat Croatia three-nil. Messi scored a penalty, then beat one of the best young defenders in the world and gave the assist to Julián Álvarez.
On the eighteenth of December 2022 Argentina played France in the final. Messi scored a penalty. Di María scored the second.
Two-nil. Ten minutes to go. Four lost finals behind, and the cup very close.
And then in less than two minutes Kylian Mbappé scored twice. Two-two.
Extra time. Messi scored again. Three-two. And then Mbappé scored once more, from a penalty. Three-three.
In the last minute France had one more chance, but Emiliano Martínez saved with his foot. And after a hundred and twenty minutes penalties decided everything.
Messi scored his. Martínez saved one, the French fluffed another. And Gonzalo Montiel walks up to the ball. This kick will decide everything.
This is that moment from the start of the film. Montiel at the ball. Messi looks at the sky and, as he later said, asks God to end it all.
Montiel scored. Lionel Messi fell to his knees on the grass.
He had lost four finals with the national team. He had said it was all over. He came back. And now, at thirty-five, he became world champion.
Before the presentation the Emir of Qatar placed a traditional black cloak on his shoulders. Messi lifted the cup, kissed it and would not let go.
Then his family came onto the pitch. His mother hugged him. His three sons ran up, and he took photos of Antonela with the cup.

His goals in the final were his sixth and seventh of the tournament. He was again given the Golden Ball. The prize that eight years earlier did not matter to him, because Argentina lost. Now he had the cup too.
At that World Cup he was the first in history to score in the group stage, the round of sixteen, the quarter-final, the semi-final and the final.
Later he said on TV that he heard the cup calling: now you can touch me.
He said he had not rewatched the final, only highlights. And at home his sons copy goalkeeper Martínez's celebrations.
In Buenos Aires millions came out onto the streets. There were so many that the team bus could not get through, and the players were taken away by helicopter.

In March 2023, before leaving Europe, he had one more happy night in Buenos Aires. In Argentina's first home match as world champions, against Panama at the Monumental, he scored the eight-hundredth goal of his career. He had always dreamed of this: celebrating with his own people, at home.

That summer, when his Paris contract ran out, he surprised everyone. Not Barcelona. Not a huge offer from Saudi Arabia. But a young club from the USA, Inter Miami. Many thought he was going there to slow down.
He explained the choice simply. He wanted to step a little out of the spotlight and think more about family. For money, he said, he would have gone to Saudi Arabia.
First match for Miami: July 2023. He came on in the second half. In the ninety-fourth minute, at one-one, he curled a free kick into the top corner.
That evening he smiled from the bench at Antonela and his sons in the stands. LeBron James and Serena Williams were there too. When the ball hit the net, club co-owner David Beckham cried.
A few weeks later Miami won the first trophy in its history. So much for slowing down. And in October, an eighth Ballon d'Or.
In Miami he also became a football dad. All three sons joined the club's academy, and he and Antonela were often seen at the touchline, like ordinary parents.
In 2024 Argentina again reached the Copa América final, against Colombia, in Miami. In the second half he twisted his ankle and left the pitch.

On the bench he cried. Next to him sat Leandro Paredes. He could not look at Leo, he said, he only heard the crying. Argentina won in extra time without him. It was also the last game of his friend Di María.

In September 2025 he played what he said was probably his last home qualifier, in Buenos Aires against Venezuela. In the warm-up he could barely hold back tears, while more than eighty thousand chanted his name. He scored twice. Finishing like this, at home, was his long-time dream, he said.
In December 2025 Miami won the MLS Cup for the first time. On the pitch his son Mateo did keepy-uppies and then pointed at his father.
In March 2026 he scored the nine-hundredth goal of his career. He was thirty-eight. Some called him an old man.
Miami did not win that match and went out of the continental cup. The result mattered more to him than the record. And ahead lay one more World Cup.
His father, Jorge, always dreamed of seeing him at one more World Cup. But just before the tournament Jorge fell seriously ill. For the first time his father would not be in the stands.
In the first game, against Algeria, he scored three goals. Then two against Austria and one against Jordan. Argentina easily won the group.
And after every game the same thing. Boots off. Phone in hand. Is there a message from home? That's how he found out how his father was.
At the time he kept silent, but played while his father lay ill thousands of kilometres away. Later he admitted that the whole tournament he felt unwell.
In the knockouts every game was a battle. Against Cape Verde, extra time.

Against Egypt Messi missed a penalty. But he did not hang his head: an assist for Romero, he equalised himself, and Enzo Fernández scored the winner with a header. Against Switzerland, extra time again.
Boots off. Phone. Word from home?

In the semi-final in Atlanta they played England. England scored first. Argentina turned it around in the last five minutes, and in the last minute Messi crossed for the winning goal. Two-one. Another final.
After the game Messi could not hold back his emotions. Then he went round the pitch hugging teammates and the whole staff. Even coach Scaloni could not find words.
At that World Cup he scored eight goals. Nobody in history had more goals and matches at World Cups.
The final took place on the nineteenth of July 2026 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The same place where ten years earlier he had said it was all over.
In the dressing room before the game he asked everyone to calm down, forget everything and think only about the game.
Spain had nineteen-year-old Lamine Yamal and a young team. For almost the whole match they had the ball, and almost all the chances.
The score was still nil-nil. In a video released later, Messi can be heard telling the team: character, guys, character.
At the end of normal time Enzo Fernández was sent off, that same boy with the letter. Ten men, and thirty more minutes.
In the hundred-and-sixth minute Ferran Torres scored. Argentina had nothing to answer with.
Messi had only one shot in the whole match. Fifth lost final with the national team.

After the whistle Messi sat on the grass. Yamal came over and hugged him. Messi told him to go his own way: the future belongs to his generation. Yamal said those words mean as much to him as a gold medal.
Scaloni broke down in tears at the press conference and left. Before the final he had called Messi the best player ever to step on a pitch.
And the next day Messi wrote to the fans. The pain is enormous, he said, and this wound needs time to heal.
Less than three weeks later, in August 2026, Jorge Messi died in Rosario after a long illness. He was sixty-eight.
A few days later Lionel wrote him a letter and showed it to the world. It began simply. I love you, Dad.

He wrote that he had promised his father to reach the final so that he would come and watch. His father never came. Lionel wanted to win and bring the cup home to him. But he could not, he wrote. His legs had nothing more to give.
And he wrote that at the World Cup after every game he waited for a message from his father. And when the messages stopped, he understood how bad things were.
You were my dad, friend and agent, he wrote. The one who left his job in Rosario and waited in Barcelona for a napkin.
Since then, looking at the sky, he saw two people there.
On the thirty-first of August he showed that message. He wrote it on the twenty-first of July, two days after the final, and kept it to himself for six weeks.
In it he said goodbye to the national team. Me vacié, he wrote. I gave everything. I have nothing more to give, and excellent young players are coming who deserve a place. Now I will be one of you.
Later he added at the end: today, after what happened with Dad, I am even more sure of the decision.
He did not write about trophies and finals. He wrote about family, about fans and about his father.

On the sixth of October 2026 he played his last match for Argentina, a friendly, against Benin, at the Monumental in Buenos Aires. This is River Plate's stadium, the club that once wanted the boy from Rosario but did not get him.
About eighty-five thousand people came. He walked out holding the hands of his three sons. His mother watched from the stands.
The anthem was performed by a Falklands War veteran. Messi could barely hold back tears. In the tenth minute the game was stopped for a long ovation, and the Benin players came over to him.
He gave two assists and scored a penalty. It was his hundred-and-twenty-sixth goal for Argentina, in his two-hundred-and-eighth match.
The second assist was for a goal by twenty-two-year-old Nico Paz, one of those young players who earned a place.
After the game hundreds of drones lit up the sky. And the boy who once sat silently in the corner of the dressing room took the microphone in front of eighty-five thousand.
First he said he was thinking of his father. And that this was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks people argued about the referees at that World Cup. Messi kept silent. And that evening he said nothing strange had happened. The team simply gave everything.
He said playing for Argentina is the best thing there can be. He would like to be here all his life. And he told the fans he loves them and will miss them.
Then he went round the pitch with his wife and three sons, while eighty-five thousand sang that Messi is not leaving.
He called it the saddest day of his career. And yet in the message he wrote: I leave in peace and with pride.
He was too small. Too expensive. A foreigner in Spain and a stranger in Argentina. Then they said he was too old.
But two people thought otherwise. The grandmother who told the coach to put him on. And the father who found the money, crossed the ocean with him and stayed.
He never played only for himself. He played for them. And looking at the sky after a goal, it is them he is looking for.
The "cold chest" Argentina talked about was not cold. He just hid his feelings. And let them out only when he lost or finally won.
And that last final, in July 2026, hurt more than all the others. It is not about the trophy. It was the last thing he wanted to bring his father.
Today he plays in Miami. He has scored more than nine hundred goals. He no longer plays for the national team. Now, as he wrote, he is just another fan.
Maybe you are a quiet one too. The one in the corner. The one people think doesn't care.
Leo was just like that. He never became loud. He spoke little. He just played, for those who believed in him. And when it mattered most, he found his voice. And one day the whole world heard him.
If you are a quiet one, you don't need to become loud. Keep playing. Your time will come.
And on the farewell evening, the boy who used to barely speak smiled at eighty-five thousand. I'm talking more than ever, he said. And I don't want to leave.
That summer Spain ended not only Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks earlier, in Texas, it shattered the dream of another boy who wanted the cup just as badly.
A boy from a small island in the Atlantic, whose teammates called him a crybaby. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his full story is right here.
